$comment: Module 4's misconception catalogue. Feeds Module 2 (agent prompt context + explanation payload) and Module 3 (OpenSearch metadata). sceneType values match /shared/scene-registry.json.

explanation.summary: Two masses released together from rest land at the same time in vacuum; air resistance is what makes real-world drops look mass-dependent.
explanation.misconception: A heavier object falls faster than a lighter one dropped from the same height.
explanation.correctModel: In the absence of air resistance, all objects near Earth's surface accelerate downward at the same rate, g ≈ 9.8 m/s², regardless of mass — gravitational force and inertial mass scale together, so mass cancels out of the acceleration.

explanation.summary: At the top of the arc, vertical velocity is momentarily zero — but horizontal velocity and downward acceleration never stop.
explanation.misconception: Velocity is zero at the top of a projectile's flight, and/or the force keeps acting along the direction of motion.
explanation.correctModel: At the apex only the vertical velocity component is zero; horizontal velocity is unchanged throughout, and the only force (ignoring drag) is gravity, acting straight down the whole time — not along the trajectory.

explanation.summary: Swap the bob for a heavier one at the same length and the period doesn't change — mass cancels out of the small-angle period formula.
explanation.misconception: A heavier pendulum bob swings faster (has a shorter period) than a lighter one.
explanation.correctModel: For small angles, period depends only on length and gravity: T = 2π√(L/g). Mass cancels because both the restoring force and the inertia it must accelerate scale together with mass.
explanation.syllabusUnit: AP Physics 1 — Unit 6: Simple Harmonic Motion

explanation.summary: There's no real outward push — only an inward pull toward the center. What feels like an outward force is your own frame lying to you.
explanation.misconception: An object moving in a circle feels an outward (centrifugal) force pushing it away from the center.
explanation.correctModel: The only real net force is centripetal — directed toward the center — and it's what bends the path into a circle. The 'outward force' is fictitious, appearing only when you analyze motion from the rotating object's own non-inertial frame.
explanation.syllabusUnit: AP Physics 1 — Unit 5: Circular Motion and Gravitation

explanation.summary: Equal masses can fully swap velocities; a light object hitting a much heavier one can bounce straight back. Mass alone doesn't decide the outcome.
explanation.misconception: In a collision, the heavier object always keeps moving forward while the lighter one just bounces off.
explanation.correctModel: The outcome is set by the mass ratio together with the two conserved quantities — momentum always, kinetic energy for an elastic collision — not by mass alone.

explanation.summary: Watch the energy bars: kinetic and elastic potential trade back and forth but their sum stays flat — nothing is 'used up' by oscillating.
explanation.misconception: The energy in an oscillating spring gets used up as it swings, which is why it eventually slows down.
explanation.correctModel: In an ideal, undamped spring-mass system total mechanical energy is conserved and continuously trades between kinetic and elastic potential energy. Real systems slow down because damping (friction, air resistance) drains energy out — oscillation itself doesn't consume it.
explanation.syllabusUnit: AP Physics 1 — Unit 6: Simple Harmonic Motion
